[MUQATIL:26:69-85/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Abraham disavows the idols as enemies, but exempts the Lord of the worlds from that disavowal.
[MUQATIL:26:69-85/r7] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The idolaters acknowledge that God created them and is their Lord, so Abraham does not disavow God.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]ماأتانيإلازيدإلاعمرا|ولايجوزالرفعفيعمرومن#392/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A second exception cannot be nominative apposition to an already excepted item, as in ما أتاني إلا زيد إلا عمرا; alternatively, one exception may be accusative and the other nominative.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]ماأتانيإلازيدإلاعمرا|ولايجوزالرفعفيعمرومن#392/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In ما أتاني إلا عمرا إلا بشرا أحد, بشر substitutes for أحد and is moved forward; the poet al-Kumayt's فما لي إلا الله غيرك ناصر supports treating غيرك like an exceptive.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]ماأتانيإلازيدإلاعمرا|ولايجوزالرفعفيعمرومن#392/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In Hāritha's verse, غير means مثل rather than an exception: only breaths remain like the corpses; a Medina-house verse is likewise read with غير as adjective or exception.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]ماأتانيإلازيدإلاعمرا|ولايجوزالرفعفيعمرومن#392/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · ابن أبي إسحاق | reports | For the Medina-house line, treating غير as an adjective permits nominative دار الخليفة; treating it as an exception requires one of the two nouns to be accusative, Ibn Abī Isḥāq's analysis.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]ماأتانيإلازيدإلاعمرا|ولايجوزالرفعفيعمرومن#392/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Repeating إلا زيد إلا أبو عبد الله is good when both names identify the same person, as emphatic repetition; it may also be a correction after a slip, with a poetic clarification as evidence.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكماليإلازيداصديقوعمراوعمروومنليإلاأباكصديقوزيدا#390/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس والخليل | reports | In مالي إلا زيدا صديق وعمرا, accusative continues the first construction; nominative makes the added name a new clause, as in وعمرو لي. Yūnus and al-Khalīl endorse both parses.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p507#2/r1] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan reads Abraham's words as saying that his people and their ancestors are his enemies, except ancestors who worshipped the Lord of the worlds.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p507#2/r2] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbī understands the exception as excluding whatever they mixed into their worship of the Lord of the worlds; those objects of worship are Abraham's enemies.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p121/r8] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The inverted phrasing فإنهم عدو لي means فإني عدو لهم, since anyone a person opposes opposes him in return.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | prefers | Although nominative and accusative forms are possible in ordinary speech, the Qur'an uses the best and most eloquent wording, ‘rabb al-ʿālamīn al-raḥmān al-raḥīm.’
[ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | ‘Al-ʿālamīn’ means everything God created, as in ‘He is Lord of everything.’ | mentions 6:164
[ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | ‘Al-ʿālamīn’ is the plural of ‘ʿālam’; the word has no singular from its own form because it gathers different kinds, while a singular ‘ʿālam’ would gather members of one kind.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh says the plural nūn is opened to distinguish it from the dual nūn, which is kasra.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The plural nūn is also opened at a meeting of two still letters; kasra is avoided as heavy after wāw or yāʾ, as in the cited forms ‘sawfa’ and ‘ayna Zayd.’
[ZAJJAJ:v4p93/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · النحويون | reports | The exception إلا رب العالمين is discontinuous, meaning but the Lord of the Worlds.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p93/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Alternatively, because the audience worshipped idols alongside God, Abraham says all they worshipped are his enemies except the Lord of the Worlds, whose worship he does not reject.
[IBNABIHATIM:v8p2779#3/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda glosses “Lord of the worlds” by reference to whatever is among His creation.
[NAHHAS:v3p182/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ applies the exception to idols alone: if Abraham worshipped them, they would be his enemies on Judgment Day.
[NAHHAS:v3p182/r7] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الفراء | reports | The singular form can represent a group; for a woman Arabs say either ‘she is an enemy of God’ or ‘she is God’s enemy.’
[NAHHAS:v3p182/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · علي بن سليمان | reports | ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān explains that the form with tāʾ means ‘hostile,’ while the form without tāʾ is treated as a relational adjective.
[NAHHAS:v3p182/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq says the exception ‘except the Lord of the worlds’ is not from the same class, but allows it to be from the class if Abraham’s people worshipped God along with idols.
[SULAMI:v2p75/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · سحنون | reports | Love becomes sound when one regards the cosmos and everything in it as an enemy, thereby loving the Beloved and withdrawing from all besides God; Abraham's words express forsaking all for connection to Him.
[HAMASA:v1p36#2/r1] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Ja'far ibn Ulba al-Harithhi's poem laments enemies overwhelming his people while women or helpless dependents were with them, people whom they were duty-bound to defend.
[HAMASA:v1p36#2/r10] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Al-mubāsil is derived from basāla, bravery; al-Marzūqi says the description agrees with the form of the singular word al-aduww rather than its meaning.
[HAMASA:v1p36#2/r2] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Al-talahhuf is grief over something lost after nearly attaining it; the source gives related exclamations and uses of the verb.
[HAMASA:v1p36#2/r3] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | reports | Ahlafa may be a singular vocative or possessive form; the possessive can shift from kasra plus ya to fatHa and alif, with comparable dialectal forms.
[HAMASA:v1p36#2/r4] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | The alif in the lament can lengthen the cry and heighten its expression of grief; al-Marzūqi compares the form with other extended vocatives and possessives.
[HAMASA:v1p36#2/r5] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Ahlabāt means helped: although the term first referred specifically to helping with milking, custom generalized it to assistance of any kind.
[HAMASA:v1p36#2/r6] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | reports | Al-walaya is the plural of waliyya, a saddlecloth; it can allude either to women or to defenseless people, while another recension reads al-mawali, meaning paternal cousins.
[HAMASA:v1p36#2/r7] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | reports | Al-Marzūqi cites the mother of Ta'abbaṭa Sharran mourning him and the saying that someone is like a discarded saddlecloth as related usages of the image.
[HAMASA:v1p36#2/r8] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | If the variant al-mawali is read, the poet singles out cousins because their estrangement hurts more, as being opposed by kin is like being fought with one's own weapon.
[HAMASA:v1p36#2/r9] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Al-Marzūqi explicitly cites the Qur'anic phrase عدو لي to illustrate the generic singular al-aduww, whose grammatical form follows the word rather than its intended collective meaning.
[THALABI:v7p166/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | “They are an enemy to me” uses a singular collective expression: every deity worshipped by Abraham’s people would be his enemy on Judgment Day; the cited verse likewise says they will disown worshippers. | mentions 19:82
[THALABI:v7p166/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra says the wording is inverted: Abraham meant “I am an enemy to them,” since someone you oppose opposes you.
[THALABI:v7p166/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra parses “except the Lord of the worlds” as an exclusion: the false gods are his enemies and not objects of worship, while he worships the Lord; another view gives the sense “rather.”
[THALABI:v7p166/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن بن الفضل | reports | Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl interpreted the exception as “the matter is with the Lord of the worlds.”
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p65#3/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi takes “they are enemies to me” as Abraham's disavowal of the idols; Maqatil paraphrases it as “I am free of them.”
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p65#3/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | Maqatil glosses the statement as “I am disavowed from them.”
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p65#3/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra explains their enmity as the idols becoming opposition and enemies to their worshippers until the Resurrection, linking this to their future disavowal of worship. | mentions 19:82
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p65#3/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutaybah calls the wording an inversion meaning “I am their enemy,” since whoever is opposed also opposes the one who opposes him.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p65#3/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-Wahidi says later writers attribute the inverted reading to al-Farra, but he has not found that attribution in al-Farra.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p65#3/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The singular noun ʿaduww may apply to a group because it is used in place of a verbal noun, so it does not take dual or plural endings; when a verbal noun is used as an adjective-as-noun, it may be inflected. | mentions 18:50, 4:92
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p66/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abu Ishaq says “except the Lord of the worlds” can be an exception outside the preceding group: Abraham worships God and does not disavow Him; alternatively, he disavows everything they worship apart from God, since they equated their idols with Him.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p66/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | Maqatil says they knew God was their Lord and Creator, and acknowledging Him as Creator counted as worship.

[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p117/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | Another explanation is that Abraham neither befriends the idols nor seeks benefit from them, as one does not with an enemy.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p233#4/r14] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The word ʿaduww can be used for plural or singular and for masculine or feminine.
